mainText: Andrew, today’s priority is Cisco Expressway. Fresh reporting says CISA has recognized exploitation of the critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting clustered Expressway Core and Edge deployments. This was already an open action in yesterday’s briefing. The change is stronger exploitation recognition, not a newly discovered vulnerability or evidence that attacks started today. Cisco’s unchanged October advisory still says it knows of no malicious use. The distinction should be made clear in customer conversations: the new CISA recognition is reported by credible journalism, while direct retrieval of CISA’s alert failed during this check. The article also contains inconsistent weekday references, so this briefing does not assert an exact catalog addition time. For affected deployments, Cisco identifies Expressway version X15.5.20 as the fixed release. Customers on X14 and earlier need to migrate to a fixed release. Cisco documents no workaround. Ask for the running build and a named owner for compromise review. A successful upgrade alone does not establish that earlier attacker access has been removed. Palo Alto’s NGINX-related advisory remains a second operational priority. The live page still lists several branch fixes with November twenty third release estimates. An estimate is not proof that a download is available. Confirm the exact branch with support, test availability after changes and retain an appropriate documented mitigation until the applicable fix is running. In Jamaica, JaCIRT’s November nineteenth warning remains a reason to check inventories for Synology DSM, LiteLLM, Apache Axis and REDCap. Healthcare, universities, government and managed service providers should retrieve the underlying advisories before closing those checks. Cayman’s warning about fraudulent speeding-fine texts remains relevant to payment verification. Additional fresh incidents across the other Caribbean territories and Latin America were not corroborated in the sources checked. Regional coverage remains incomplete, and no local victims are inferred. Take three account actions. First, identify clustered Expressway estates, obtain fixed-build evidence and assign compromise-review owners. Second, verify actual availability of the correct Palo Alto branch fixes, test changes and keep appropriate mitigation in place until remediation is complete. Third, close cloud and regional carryovers with evidence: Rackspace secret rotation, Entra tenant and sign-in review, vCenter investigation and JaCIRT inventory checks. Reinforce independent verification of payment requests with staff and customers.
